practice_items.atom_title: TCP/IP fundamentals and network topology flaws
practice_items.prompt: Which TCP/IP layer is responsible for routing packets between networks using IP addresses?
options: Application layer
Transport layer
Internet layer
Network access layer
practice_items.explain: The internet layer (IP) assigns addresses and routes packets between networks. The transport layer manages ports and reliability; the network access layer handles local delivery using MAC addresses.

practice_items.atom_title: TCP/IP fundamentals and network topology flaws
practice_items.prompt: Which of the following are structural weaknesses built into TCP/IP that attackers exploit? Select ALL that apply.
options: IP addresses are not authenticated
DNS caches can accept forged replies
TCP uses encrypted sequence numbers by default
ARP operates on trust with no authentication
practice_items.explain: IP has no source-address verification (spoofing), DNS caches forgeable replies (poisoning), and ARP trusts any reply broadcast (ARP spoofing). TCP sequence numbers are NOT encrypted by default, that is a weakness, not a safeguard.

practice_items.atom_title: TCP/IP fundamentals and network topology flaws
practice_items.prompt: An attacker floods a switch with thousands of fake MAC addresses until it begins broadcasting all frames to every port. What attack is this?
options: MAC flooding
IP spoofing
ARP poisoning
DNS spoofing
practice_items.explain: MAC flooding exhausts the switch's CAM table, forcing it to broadcast like a hub, enabling passive sniffing of all frames.

practice_items.atom_title: TCP/IP fundamentals and network topology flaws
practice_items.prompt: What network design practice limits how far an attacker can move laterally after compromising a single internal host?
practice_items.explain: Network segmentation (VLANs, subnets with controlled routing) contains a breach to one zone, preventing a compromised host from reaching all others.

practice_items.atom_title: TCP/IP fundamentals and network topology flaws
practice_items.prompt: During a TCP three-way handshake, what is the correct order of messages?
options: ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK
SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK
SYN-ACK, SYN, ACK
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
practice_items.explain: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, the client completes with ACK. Early implementations used predictable sequence numbers, enabling session hijacking.

practice_items.atom_title: TCP/IP fundamentals and network topology flaws
practice_items.prompt: Which layer of the TCP/IP stack does IP spoofing primarily target?
options: Application layer
Transport layer
Internet layer
Network access layer
practice_items.explain: IP spoofing forges the source address field in the IP header, which lives at the internet layer. Defenses (ingress filtering) also operate at this layer.

practice_items.prompt: Why can an attacker forge a DNS response over UDP more easily than they could tamper with a TCP connection?
options: UDP responses are digitally signed by default
UDP always encrypts responses
UDP requires the attacker to be on the same physical cable
UDP is connectionless, so there is no handshake the resolver can use to verify the reply's origin
practice_items.explain: DNS over UDP is a single stateless query/reply pair; the resolver has no session state to verify the reply actually came from the authoritative server, so a correctly-guessed forged reply is accepted.

practice_items.prompt: Which THREE fields must a forged DNS reply match for a resolver to accept it as the answer to an outstanding query?
options: TTL, checksum, and MAC address
Source IP address only
Destination port, query domain name, transaction ID
HTTP status code, cookie, and referrer
practice_items.explain: The resolver checks the reply's transaction ID, source port (the port it sent the query from), and query name against the outstanding query before accepting the answer.

practice_items.prompt: Which of the following are effective defenses against DNS cache poisoning? Select ALL that apply.
options: Source port randomization
DNSSEC cryptographic signatures
Hiding the resolver's IP address
Increasing the TTL of all records to one week
practice_items.explain: Source port randomization widens the guessing space an attacker must brute-force, and DNSSEC lets a resolver cryptographically verify a reply even if an attacker wins the UDP race. Hiding the resolver's IP and raising TTLs do not address the underlying spoofing vulnerability.

practice_items.prompt: In the Kaminsky attack, why does the attacker query unique, non-existent subdomains (e.g. 1.bank.com, 2.bank.com) instead of the base domain?
options: It is required by the DNS protocol specification
It bypasses DNSSEC entirely
It forces the resolver to issue a fresh query to the authoritative server every time, since there is no cached answer, giving the attacker repeated chances to win the race
It reduces the number of packets the attacker needs to send
practice_items.explain: A unique subdomain guarantees a cache miss, forcing a new query-and-race cycle each time, which multiplies the attacker's opportunities to guess the transaction ID before the real reply arrives.

practice_items.prompt: Name the DNS extension that adds cryptographic signatures so a resolver can verify a reply even if an attacker wins the UDP timing race.
practice_items.explain: DNSSEC signs DNS records with a key hierarchy rooted at the DNS root zone, letting resolvers reject unsigned or incorrectly signed forged replies.

practice_items.prompt: A resolver's outstanding query has tx_id=500 and source port=9000. A reply arrives with tx_id=500, port=9000, but for a different query name than was asked. What should the resolver do?
options: Cache it anyway since the tx_id matches
Reject the reply as a mismatch
Cache it anyway since the port matches
Forward it to the authoritative server for verification
practice_items.explain: All three fields (tx_id, port, AND query name) must match; a mismatched query name means this reply does not answer the outstanding query and must be rejected.

practice_items.prompt: Why does ARP allow spoofing so easily?
options: ARP requires a password for every reply
ARP replies must be digitally signed by the gateway
ARP only works over encrypted channels
ARP has no built-in authentication, so any device can send a reply and it will be trusted
practice_items.explain: ARP was designed for a small trusted network in 1982 and has no cryptographic authentication, any host can send a reply (even unsolicited) and receiving hosts will update their ARP table.

practice_items.prompt: An attacker wants to intercept all of a victim's internet-bound traffic on a LAN using ARP spoofing. Which two devices' ARP tables does the attacker typically poison?
options: Two random unrelated hosts on the network
The victim's and the default gateway's
Only the DNS server's
Only the victim's web browser cache
practice_items.explain: To intercept traffic between the victim and the internet, the attacker poisons the victim's ARP table (to point 'gateway' at the attacker) and the gateway's ARP table (to point 'victim' at the attacker), placing itself in the middle of that path.

practice_items.prompt: Which of the following are effective technical controls against ARP spoofing? Select ALL that apply.
options: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches
Static ARP entries for critical hosts like the gateway
Renaming the Wi-Fi network's SSID
Network segmentation with VLANs
practice_items.explain: DAI validates ARP against a trusted binding table, static entries prevent the OS from accepting a forged update for a specific IP, and VLAN segmentation limits which hosts share a broadcast domain (and thus can spoof each other). Renaming an SSID has no effect on ARP spoofing.

practice_items.prompt: Does HTTPS fully prevent damage from a successful ARP-spoofing man-in-the-middle position?
options: Yes, HTTPS makes MITM positioning impossible
No, HTTPS provides no protection at all against MITM
No, HTTPS protects the confidentiality/integrity of the payload, but the attacker can still see which servers are contacted and can attempt downgrade or certificate-warning attacks
Yes, once ARP is poisoned, HTTPS automatically re-routes traffic safely
practice_items.explain: HTTPS does not stop the attacker from occupying the MITM position via ARP spoofing; it limits what the attacker can do with that position (cannot read/alter the encrypted payload without detection), but metadata like destination server and connection timing remain visible, and downgrade/certificate attacks are still possible against unwary users.

practice_items.prompt: Name the switch-level feature that validates ARP packets against a trusted IP-to-MAC binding table and drops forged ones.
practice_items.explain: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) uses a trusted binding table (often built from DHCP snooping records) to validate and drop ARP packets that don't match a legitimate binding.

practice_items.prompt: An ARP-watch tool observes IP 192.168.1.1 first bound to MAC aa:11, then 40 seconds later sees a reply claiming 192.168.1.1 is at MAC bb:22. How should this be classified?
options: SPOOFED, a different MAC now claims an IP that was already bound to a different MAC
LEGIT, ARP bindings change routinely
Cannot be determined without a packet capture
LEGIT, only DNS bindings can be spoofed, not ARP
practice_items.explain: A second, different MAC claiming an already-bound IP is exactly the ARP spoofing signature that arpwatch-style tools flag.

practice_items.prompt: What NIC setting must a capture tool typically use to see traffic not addressed to its own MAC address?
options: DHCP mode
Airplane mode
Promiscuous mode
Bridge mode
practice_items.explain: Promiscuous mode tells the network stack to accept and process every frame the NIC physically receives, not just frames addressed to its own MAC, necessary for a capture tool to see traffic beyond its own.

practice_items.prompt: What is the difference between a capture filter and a display filter in a tool like Wireshark?
options: They are the same thing with different names
A capture filter determines what is recorded at all; a display filter narrows the view of what was already captured
A display filter determines what is recorded; a capture filter only changes colors
Capture filters only work on Windows
practice_items.explain: A capture filter is applied before/during capture and discards non-matching packets permanently; a display filter is applied afterward to a full capture and only changes what is shown, not what was recorded.

practice_items.prompt: Which of the following protocols send credentials in plaintext, making them fully readable in a packet capture? Select ALL that apply.
options: Telnet
HTTPS
FTP (control channel)
SSH
practice_items.explain: Telnet and FTP's control channel send authentication data in cleartext. HTTPS and SSH both encrypt the connection, so credentials are not readable in a capture.

practice_items.prompt: On a fully switched (non-hub) network, which technique lets an attacker still see another host's traffic without physical access to a SPAN port?
options: Renaming their hostname
Simply plugging into any switch port
Changing their own IP address
ARP spoofing to redirect the victim's traffic through the attacker's machine
practice_items.explain: A switch normally isolates traffic to the correct destination port; ARP spoofing (3.1.c) tricks two hosts into routing traffic through the attacker, restoring visibility that switching would otherwise prevent.

practice_items.prompt: Name the legitimate switch feature, intended for monitoring tools, that copies traffic from one or more ports to a monitoring port, and which becomes a risk if granted to the wrong party.
practice_items.explain: Port mirroring (a SPAN port) duplicates traffic to a monitoring port for legitimate analysis; if misconfigured or given to an unauthorized party, it enables unauthorized sniffing.

practice_items.prompt: A capture log entry shows TCP port 443 traffic to a banking site with payload described only as encrypted binary data. What should an analyst conclude?
options: No credential can be extracted from this capture because TLS encrypts the payload
The password is visible if you look closely enough
Port 443 is always cleartext
This is definitely a Telnet session
practice_items.explain: Port 443 (HTTPS) encrypts the payload end-to-end; even if login data is being transmitted, the captured bytes are unreadable ciphertext without the decryption key.
